prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: National Airspace System (NAS), Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), airspace users, aircraft, pilots, air traffic controllers, traffic managers, stakeholders, ground/aircraft automation; air traffic management (ATM).
Current ATM uses approved flight plans/departures; sparse data, unpublished changes, unsynchronized predictions, unknown constraints, and open-ended clearances impair prediction. Disruptions create route-amendment backlogs; downstream effects are poorly predicted. Ground Delay Programs (GDPs)/Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) target Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) using user-estimated en-route times; Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) assumes accurate estimated times of arrival (ETAs).
Management by Trajectory (MBT) applies to all Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) aircraft. FAA/users negotiate and assign closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs), current state to destination, respecting user goals and every applicable constraint. All aircraft follow assigned trajectories and comply with trajectory constraints. Pilots/controllers use automation for compliance; equipped aircraft bear substantial responsibility. Constraint tolerances reflect individual flight performance and situational need. Supported operations include commercial aviation, Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, and on-demand air transportation vehicles.
NAS Constraint Service publishes common static/dynamic NAS constraints to all stakeholders. Trajectory constraints map to NAS constraints, identifying affected aircraft when constraints change. Publish every trajectory change; relevant users, aircraft, and FAA automation receive information enabling accurate, synchronized predictions. Traffic managers apply constraints to amend trajectories as events evolve; constraint-selection details are unspecified. Consider downstream effects in all trajectory decisions, including tactical actions; modify trajectories early and proactively.
Quantified time-based performance complements Performance Based Navigation (PBN) metrics, enabling one efficient ATM concept for all IFR aircraft with acceptable safety risk. Time of arrival control (TOAC) certification thresholds risk mixed equipage, separate concepts, and unacceptable risk.
Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) is the broader 4DT-centered vision; MBT interprets it consistently with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidance and resembles four-dimensional (4D) contracts.

New part:
U0051: Traffic management automation will identify which flights are affected by each TMI and translate that TMI into one or more trajectory constraints specific to the flight.  Aircraft provide detailed information about their predicted 4DT (a.k.a. intent data) that is shared across stakeholders.
U0052: Aircraft provide updates when intent data change.  Conflicts can be detected further in advance due to improved predictability, and intervention can be accomplished through adding or modifying constraints in the assigned 4DT.  Open trajectories (i.e., tactical vectoring by controllers) for which the controller’s and/or pilot’s intent is unknown by other actors in the system are minimized.  MBT follows two paths to eliminating open trajectories: 1) introducing methods for planning tactical maneuvers as closed trajectory modifications and 2) eliminating the need for tactical maneuvers through improved predictability.  Digital air-ground communication is used to deliver 4DTs to aircraft cockpits for easy loading and execution in the Flight Management System (FMS).  Broadband air-ground communications and advanced electronic flight bag (EFB) applications are used to include the flight crew in the trajectory negotiation process.  A negotiating controller subsumes the responsibilities of the D-side controller.
U0053: Together, the negotiating controller and traffic management coordinators (TMCs), with their longer time horizon perspectives, proactively intervene to avoid conflicts and achieve TFM objectives, using automation enhancements that facilitate coordinating 4DT changes across multiple sectors. 1.3 Purpose This document is intended to describe a far-term MBT concept.
U0054: Far-term is not precisely defined but targets an operational environment in which the NAS, and the vast majority of aircraft, are capable of the advanced data exchange and automation capabilities associated with the Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2).
U0055: The value of this document is to provide a vector to guide research. 1.4 Near- vs.
U0056: Far-Term MBT This MBT Concept of Operations (ConOps) presents an end-state vision for MBT, while beginning to identify what could be feasible in the more near-term timeframe.
U0057: The near- and far- term MBT concepts differ in two ways.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
